Editor’s Note

Neal Vorus

Neal Vorus

Neal Vorus  

Since its inception at the close of the 19th century, psychoanalysis has been a field defined by a tension running between certainty and the unknown, orthodoxy and innovation. In our clinical practice we offer patients the opportunity to know their mind in all its complexity by providing a medium for radically free expression, the achievement of which requires the analyst to embrace an openness to the not-yet-known. And yet, ironically, the history of our field is punctuated by periodic clashes of orthodoxy, of warring absolutisms. It is perhaps to be expected that confrontation with the unknowable so often elicits a ceaseless yearning for certainty, a hunger for orthodoxy, particularly during times of heightened anxiety.

Alongside the proliferation of the multiplicity of ideas that deepen our understanding, the continuation of our profession as a coherent discipline depends on what Joseph Sandler (1983) once described as the “very necessary conservative trend” (p. 35) that resists change and holds us together. The tension between tradition and innovation, coherence and disjunction, security and patience (Bion 1970) has shaped the evolution of our discipline from the start. It is now over seventy-five years since the Freud-Klein controversies erupted within organized psychoanalysis while war raged across the continent. It was a battle between orthodoxies out of which emerged a creative tension that allowed for the return of the unknown in the form (ultimately) of Bion’s O and Winnicott’s (1963) “music of the spheres” (p. 192).

To remain vital, psychoanalytic publications need to continually rediscover the balance point between tradition and change in our field. We are a discipline, perhaps more than any other, that grounds itself in the writings and discoveries of its founder. Michael Diamond

Michael Diamond

Michael Diamond   Training and Supervising Analyst, Los Angeles Institute and Society for Psychoanalytic Studies, where he teaches and supervises. He has authored several books, including Ruptures in the American Psyche: Containing Destructive Populism in Perilous Times (2022) and Masculinity and Its Discontents: The Male Psyche and the Inherent Tensions of Maturing Manhood (2021).
Fascistic states, omnipotence, destructive narcissism, large group regression, unconscious fantasies, annihilation anxieties, death drive, purification, malignant leadership, paranoid-schizoid position, perverted containment, authoritarianism

To understand fascistic group movements, it is necessary to understand the dynamics of fascistic states of mind within all of us. Following a note on the American polity, the author differentiates fascism from authoritarianism before reviewing the dynamics of fascistic states of mind, including the omnipotent longing for purity and its relationship to destructive narcissism. Considering the role of the death drive, the allure of the fascistic state is explored, based largely in the need to avoid primary terrors of annihilation. In addressing the movement of such states from the individual psyche to the larger group mind, the author examines the symbiotic fit between the leader and the group’s unconscious fears and phantasies, as illustrated by perverse containment within the cult of Trumpism. Finally, in noting the inability of reason alone to contain destructive forces, he ponders how we might deal with fascistic states of mind most effectively in individuals, groups, and ourselves.

J. David Miller   Supervising and Training Analyst at the Washington Baltimore Center for Psychoanalysis and a Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the George Washington University Medical School. He has a clinical practice in Washington, DC. His published papers explore the interface of psychoanalysis and art.
Vermeer, art, Freud, Kris, Klein, Segal, Kohut, Loewald, pluralism, creative process

Vermeer’s masterpiece, “The Allegory of Painting,” which is the one work that he refused to sell, brings to mind the successful outcome of psychoanalytic treatment. In its incongruities, this painting presumably contains and reflects the conflicted inner world of the artist, but it also evokes a remarkable sense of coherence and harmony. To develop a credible explanation for Vermeer’s achievement in analytic terms, I found it helpful to employ several major theoretical models; this finding suggests that for clinical analysis as well, a multi-theory approach would be optimal.

Made for the trainee analyst, Lessons in Psychoanalysis: Psychopathology and Clinical Psychoanalysis for Trainee Analysts by Franco De Masi is a unique contribution. There is already quite a voluminous literature1 that comprehensively covers many of the topics in De Masi’s book. So, how does one add to it without almost inevitably overlapping with others?

Unlike previous books covering similar ground and that take an academic approach in reviewing what psychoanalysis is as a discipline, Lessons in Psychoanalysis, written in the voice of the author, reflects De Masi’s personal take on different concepts in psychoanalysis–-clinical and theoretical alike. In fact, the author presents a very subjective account of what psychoanalysis is for him. The emphasis on the subjective starts with the opening paragraphs of the book and continues through the author’s personalized journey through various psychoanalytic concepts.

De Masi speaks with authority–-authority developed through years of clinical experience–-on subjects that many readers will find useful: basic tenets of psychoanalysis, diagnostic taxonomy, clinical and technical strategies, and the history of psychoanalysis. Theoretical concepts, psychoanalytic history and clinical experience crystallize in numerous observations, insights, and unique theoretical integrations. As I approached the task of reviewing Melanie Klein: A Contemporary Introduction, I was wondering what might make this book particular in its explication of Kleinian concepts. There are a variety of such books at this point, variously depicting Melanie Klein’s world and her ideas. I say this to make clear that I was a bit doubtful at first, even while intrigued. Having now read Penelope Garvey’s focused, clear, and comprehensive overview of Melanie Klein’s principal ideas, I very much appreciate the particularity of her contribution. Garvey is doing something the other introductory works have not done in quite the same way.

In six highly concentrated and distinct chapters, Garvey describes in clear and accessible language the evolution of Klein’s ideas. Garvey places Klein’s formation in historical time and situates the unfolding of her ideas in relation to her own life history. The author sets it up so that Klein’s personal history comes alive with brief references to her biography that help to ground and enrich our appreciation of Klein’s person along with her theory. Early losses (of her brother and then her father) are noted as central to Klein’s preoccupation with mourning along with war which constitutes the backdrop against which many of Klein’s theories are further developed and elaborated. In describing this, Garvey is attempting to counter the misperception (often stated) that Klein ignored external reality. Many years ago, a woman came to my office for a consultation, ostensibly about a low dose of anti-anxiety medication that she used occasionally. She was meticulously dressed and gently mannered, and fairly soon after arriving she mentioned that three months prior she’d had sexual reassignment surgery and had been transitioning with hormones and feminizing her public presentation for two years. She was not yet divorced from her wife, and their three children ranging in age from fifteen to twenty years of age were responding reasonably well to the transition of their father to womanhood. Days before she consulted me, her estranged wife had been diagnosed with a cancer that would likely be fatal, which she saw as a tragedy that opened the opportunity for her to take a more actively nurturing role with her children. She described her desire to be more personally involved as a departure from her previous ways of relating to her children as a more distant father, and attributed the change to estrogen. She felt kinder, gentler, and stated plainly, “Estrogen is the source of all nurturing.”

When I quoted this patient’s statement about estrogen in a psychoanalytic classroom, one of the participants quickly implored, “Where can I get some of that stuff for my mother?” After a laugh, we tried to sort out which aspects of gender and sex could still be seen as biological or essential realities, and which former realities are upended by the lived experiences of patients in our offices and others in the world around us.

Larry Sandberg

Larry Sandberg   Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry at Weill Cornell Medical Center and Lecturer at Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research.
Somatic narration, encapsulated body engram, gaze aversion, psychosis, embodiment, nonverbal communication

The utility of Sebastian Leikert’s technical approach of somatic narration is illustrated in a detailed clinical presentation working with a psychotic patient with gaze aversion. In conjunction with Riccardo Lombardi’s emphasis on focusing on the patient’s transference to her own body rather than the conventional transference to the analyst, the author shows the value of moving away from gaze aversion and focusing, instead, on the patient’s experience of her neck as an encapsulated body engram. The role of bodily movement in the consulting room as a critical ingredient in supporting the narrative process will be illustrated.

Employing an applied psychoanalytic lens to Spike Jonze’s her (2013), this paper expands on meaning-making opportunities available to the film. Such expansion is pursued by focusing additional attention to cinematic strategies and language, attended to by a psychoanalytic appreciation of object relations and Andre Green’s thoughts on negation. With such considerations in place, the paper further articulates unconscious material pertinent to the film and culture at large, as it better appreciates the developmental crisis endured by the film’s protagonist.

The Concept of Erasure in Second Generation Holocaust Survivors’ Art and in Psychoanalysis

Hilit Erel-Brodsky

Hilit Erel-Brodsky

Mevòot 72
Savyon, Israel
5651058
hilitbr@gmail.com

Hilit Erel-Brodsky   Clinical social worker, didactic psychoanalyst and supervisor, Israeli Psychoanalytic Society. She is also the Chair of the Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy Program, Bar Ilan University.
Erasure, memory, Holocaust, disassociation, art, trauma, pentimento

Is the erasure of memories truly possible? What existed prior to this erasure, and what remains afterward? In this paper, I will explore the concept of erasure within the art of second-generation, Holocaust survivor artists and its implications in psychoanalysis, particularly examining its connection to the phenomenon of dissociation among these individuals. I will distinguish between two types of pathological dissociation through second-generation, Holocaust survivor artists: one in which a link between different states of consciousness is preserved, allowing individuals to experience phantom pain, and another type where symptoms are less accessible for processing and analytical work. In the latter case, these symptoms are primarily sensorial and primal, which calls for a specific set of clinical recommendations. Additionally, the paper will outline strategies for clinical responses to trauma experienced by second-generation Holocaust survivors.

François Ansermet   Professor Emeritus of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry at the University of Geneva and at the University of Lausanne; former Director of the Department of psychiatry, University of Geneva; former Head of the Department of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, University Hospital of Geneva and psychoanalyst; and a member of the Word Association of Psychoanalysis.
Genetics, heredity, Freud, aetiology, inter-disciplinarity, psychoanalysis history

To emphasize how interwoven innate and acquired factors are in the aetiology of mental disorders, Freud introduced the concept of complemental series. Today, current genetic research data is shedding new light on this hypothesis. The development of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has highlighted the interaction of genetic and environmental factors in the aetiology of psychiatric diseases. By reinterpreting the evolution of Freud’s positions regarding the aetiological role of heredity through the prism of current literature, this article aims to introduce a dialogue between psychoanalysis and contemporary genetics.

Knowing What Psychoanalysts Do and Doing What Psychoanalysts Know may well be the most important book in our field that readers will come across in many years. It may also prove to be one of the most informative, useful, and challenging books that they are likely to encounter. Over fifty years ago, at his London IPA Congress presentation, André Green1 attempted to address what was then felt to be a crisis in psychoanalysis. Today, looking around at the diminished place that psychoanalysis currently holds in our health care system and general culture, the conflicts within and between our organizations, and the nature and level of the disparities in practice and theory that exist, it is difficult not to conclude that the crisis still persists and may even have worsened.

Although it may prove rather unpopular to say so, I think that one important contribution to the crisis has been the failure of organized psychoanalysis to really identify, explore, and think and talk seriously about the differences that exist between various psychoanalytic theories, models and practices, and the many local, regional, and language group iterations of those theories, models, and practices. Nina Marion Blackett was born in Kensington, London, on February 1, 1900 and is known by her husband Dennis Milner’s surname, but also as Marion Blackett-Milner. After studying at University College (London) and graduating in 1924 with a degree in psychology, she became known as the pioneer of introspective journalism under the pseudonym Joanna Field.

Her first occupations were in the field of career guidance and occupational psychology at the National Institute of Industrial Psychology. At the same time, she engaged in introspective analysis and wrote the book A Life of One’s Own in 1934 as Marion Milner, which was appreciated by Wystan Hugh Auden and Stephen Spender. Her next book, A Life of One’s Own: An Experiment in Leisure (1937) was written under the pseudonym of Joanna Field; and continuing her autobiographical writing, fifty years later she published Eternity’s Sunrise: A Way of Keeping a Diary (1987).

Igor Kolmakov   Holds a private practice in Tel Aviv (Israel) and currently works at Geha Mental Health Centre. His research deals with the history and philosophy of psychotherapy (and psychology in general), clinical epistemology, as well as the notions of “mental health” and “mental illness.”
Freud, psychoanalysis, epistemology, phronesis, abduction, methodology, Sherlock Holmes, conjecture, narrative, clues, detective

Although the comparison between two great Victorian masterminds, Sigmund Freud and Sherlock Holmes, and their respective methods, is in itself not new (see for example Ginzburg 1979, 1980; Brooks 1984; Marcus 1984; Shephard 1985; Spence 1987), it merits further investigation, as it raises important questions regarding the nature and structure of clinical evidence, clinical epistemology, and clinical narration. In this article, the author: refers both to the common cultural background of these two projects (including the disenchantment of the modern world and the complicated dialog between rationality and imagination) and their common epistemological situation; analyses their search for a plot and search for clues, and characterizes both Holmes and Freud as applied historians and applied semioticians. Their modi operandi are described as hermeneutical procedures, methodologically similar to Charles Sanders Peirce’s abduction. Moreover, the author argues that both can be viewed as manifestations of Aristotle’s phronesis. Finally, the author points out one important difference between Freud and Holmes, namely that in fact the Viennese Holmes is at the same time the Viennese Watson.

Isaac Jean-Francois   Fifth-year doctoral candidate in the joint degree program of African American and American Studies at Yale University. His published work explores aesthetics, phenomenology, Black Studies, and Queer Studies.
Skin, trauma, desire, sexuality, race

Black Studies and psychoanalysis both consider how socio-sexual dynamics contour the skin. Black Studies scholar Hortense Spillers (1987) alongside psychoanalytic theorist Didier Anzieu (1985) trace the skin as a porous enclosure, albeit in different discursive environments. Also a scholar of psychoanalysis, Spillers’s work emphasizes the intersubjective nature of embodiment: history carries notions of race, which frames interactions between desiring subjects. As a case study, the journals of writer and English doctoral student Gary Fisher (1961-1994) provide a narrative surface to place both traditions in conversation. This article investigates the fraught relationship between the imagined and historical in the psyche’s processing of racial trauma. Fisher’s exploration of his racialized fantasies and sexuality unfurls across his writing at the height of the HIV/AIDS epidemic, an epidemic which continues today. Fisher’s prose reveals that abject sexual practices, those which rely on racial tropes to efface and excite the desiring subject, can inspire meaningful self-actualization and broaden understandings of race and sexuality.

Lucy LaFarge (1948–2025)

Wendy Katz and Daria Colombo

Daria Colombo

dcolombo8@gmail.com

Daria Colombo  

Lucy Bergson LaFarge died on February 20, 2025. Faced with a recurrence of cancer only months after the most painful loss of her son, the acclaimed novelist Paul La Farge, Lucy had resolved to pursue her treatment with optimism and to make the most of what remained of her life with fortitude, as Paul had done. Stepping away from her position as Editor in Chief at the Quarterly, a role she had embraced only three years earlier with her characteristic mix of enthusiasm, diligence, and creativity, was another loss; but those who knew Lucy best were not surprised by her decision to focus her remaining energy on the patients she was still analyzing and on making the most of her time with her husband, Richard Zimmer, and their beloved Labradoodle, YoFi. Lucy was widely known to be an insatiable and discerning reader. Her love of literature was a solace, with many of her conversations with friends during this time centered on soliciting book recommendations and comparing opinions about the latest novels. At all times, she was shadowed by YoFi, the most recent, the most devoted, and perhaps even the best of the best in the long line of Lucy’s and Rick’s very good dogs.

Lucy Ann Bergson was born in New York City on September 3, 1948, the youngest of three daughters of Abram Bergson and Rita Macht Bergson. Her father was an internationally renowned economist and Sovietologist as well as a professor at Columbia University, where years later Lucy herself would join the faculty and become a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research. Her mother was a school psychologist. When Lucy was young, the family moved to Cambridge where her father joined the faculty at Harvard. A precocious and creative child, Lucy’s interest in psychoanalytic thinking was nurtured by an early acquaintance with Eleanor Galenson, whose brother was a colleague of Lucy’s father.

The title of this book, when read without the subtitle, would of course, make the reader immediately think they were encountering a book about our current president-elect, Donald J. Trump. Any anticipation of such immediacy and relevance is quickly converted, as conveyed by the subtitle, into a study of a much earlier president, Woodrow Wilson, who is largely unknown to today’s readers and the unexpected “madman” of the title. The average reader will undoubtedly be surprised at such an assessment of Wilson as a madman president. As presidents go, Wilson’s reputation has grown in stature since his presidential years. Apparently, during his two terms from 1912 to 1920 his involvement in World War I and in particular his role in the treaty of Versailles was the cause of much public consternation. Wilson had assumed a large role in the negotiations for the treaty of Versailles which he linked to the establishment of a league of nations that would ensure perpetual world peace. His was the plan to end war for all time. However, as presented by this author, his actions and stubbornness, as well as his hatred of the Republican Senator Henry Cabot Lodge, resulted in the failure of the Senate to ratify the treaty. At the time this outcome was seen as cataclysmic.

It is in this setting that the dramatic narrative of this volume needs to be understood. It is very much linked to psychoanalysis through a connection between an American diplomat, William Bullitt, a figure of enormous, if concealed, importance in diplomatic history for most of the twentieth century. Eve Watson

Eve Watson  

Readers should not be deceived by the title of this 1968-1969 seminar which is Lacan’s sixteenth in a series of twenty-seven over the course of his lifetime’s work. Coming as it does after The Psychoanalytic Act and immediately prior to the more well-known The Other Side of Psychoanalysis where he develops his theory of the four discourses, this seminar, while about the Other, places its emphasis on the subject, and offers a centralization henceforth of the subject in Lacan’s teaching. The seminar should also be placed, and this will be of interest to non-Lacanian readers, in the context of serious social upheaval in France and in psychoanalytic institutions and universities which were reforming in the late 1960s. Afoot was serious unrest in Lacan’s own school, the École Freudienne de Paris, which was revising its process for formally designating psychoanalysts within its procedure called the “Pass.” Lacan, true to form, was against any standardization in which formation could be linked to a conjunction of knowledge and power, and because senior members of the school—the old guard—were being overlooked by the new Pass procedures, dissent and trouble were swirling and a split was in the offing. The younger generation attending Lacan’s lectures was more radical and revolution was the air. They sought a purer Lacanianism freed from its Freudian origins.1 Against this backdrop of social and institutional unrest, and what Lacan perceived to be stagnation within his own psychoanalytic group, this seminar is directed to a teaching about how psychoanalysis should be taught and transmitted.

The Psychoanalytic Quarterly is pleased to welcome Neal Vorus as Editor-in-Chief, effective February 1, 2025.

Analytic process is a poorly understood concept often thought to have an agreed upon meaning despite evidence to the contrary. So long as it remains ill-defined, its value as a metric of both candidate progression and whether a presented case demonstrates said process is dubious. The author describes her emotional reactions and counter-transferences in ending analyses in lieu of her personal situation, in which she was anticipating retirement. Through a clinical case of a patient who had difficulties in ending treatment, and her own dream which occurred during this time, the author shows how both she and the patient shared unconscious fantasies about aging and stopping the passage of time. The analyst’s resistances about retiring from clinical practice in concert with the patient’s resistances about ending analysis created a barrier against analytic progress. Endings, termination, resistance of the analyst, post-treatment contact, remote analysis

This introductory essay provides an integrative summary and critical analysis of seven papers on endings in psychoanalysis. There is strong agreement regarding the essential individuality of each ending, rather than any usual criteria that apply to some but not to all endings of treatment. Recent developments in analytic theory and practice that focus on early trauma, dissociation, and the need for development of missing and inadequate structures and capacities raise new and newly emphasized questions regarding analytic endings. The advantages and disadvantages of different forms of post-treatment contact are considered, as are the implications of remotely conducted analysis. The analyst’s resistance to ending emerges as a consistent emphasis in this series of papers.

The purpose of this paper is to reformulate the concept of interpretation in a way that better reflects the interpsychic and processive dimensions of this concept as increasingly represented in psychoanalytic writings. Implicit in my redefinition is the view that, while the interpretive process is essential to therapeutic action, the notion of making interpretations is an artificial and problematic way of viewing the work of analysis. In this paper I will review an expanded definition of interpretation as developed through the writings of Hans Loewald and elaborated by more contemporary thinkers such as Sheldon Bach, Ronald Britton, and Antonino Ferro.

Lucy LaFarge stepped down as editor-in-chief (EIC) of the Psychoanalytic Quarterly due to illness in June of 2024, following an unexpectedly brief, three-year tenure. During this short but very productive period as EIC, Lucy initiated a new, collaborative editorial model incorporating four associate editors; worked to generate new ethical guidelines for the protection of patients’ confidentiality in published clinical work; and guided the publication of numerous regular and special issues (the latter included topics such as psychoanalysis during the pandemic, neutrality, and identity). With this work, Lucy gathered some of the most distinguished and creative writers in our field, bringing them into conversation on important theoretical and clinical subjects both enduring and timely. She brought tremendous enthusiasm and commitment to this role, and her tenure importantly marked the first time a woman held the position of editor-in-chief.

Lucy took up the mantle of editor-in-chief with a strong guiding vision of the Quarterly as a journal that should focus on the publication of excellent scholarship about clinical psychoanalysis. Having honed her editorial skills for more than a decade at the International Journal of Psychoanalysis as book review editor and then as Regional Editor for North America, she brought a careful, rigorous, and highly generative spirit to working with authors, reviewers, and associate editors. The Quarterly’s uncommon culture of independence, excellence, and collaborative intellectual and clinical inquiry owes a great deal to Lucy’s contributions.

Anne Hoffman

Anne Hoffman

hoffman.leon@gmail.com

Anne Hoffman   Professor Emerita of English and Comparative Literature at Fordham University. She is a member of the faculty of the NY Psychoanalytic Institute and the research faculty of the DeWitt Wallace Institute for Psychiatry: History, Policy, and the Arts.
Infantile sexuality, unconscious fantasy, narrative, Nachträglichkeit, Henry James, Sigmund Freud

At the intersection of literature and psychoanalysis, this essay draws on Freud’s discovery of the infantile sexual unconscious to explore moments in the late novels of Henry James, in which an adult protagonist both recognizes and disavows the visible evidence of a sexual relationship. The essay considers Hans Holbein’s 1533 painting, The Ambassadors, as a possible source for Henry James’ choice of title for his 1903 novel: the painting’s visual play with point of view touches on the narrative disavowal of what is there to be seen. The essay explores some narrative dimensions of Freud’s writing to highlight the dynamic disclosure of the infantile within the adult. The concept of Nachträglichkeit, recognizing the deferred or belated impact of disruptive recurrences in mental life, helps to understand such moments and gives insight, more broadly, into narrative experience. Drawing on Nachträglichkeit as a principle of mental life, the essay explores the resonances of infantile sexuality, fantasy, and trauma in narrative, and more generally, as a resource in creative expression.

The Infantile in Psychoanalytic Practice Today is the first-ever translation of Florence Guignard’s now classic work, Au vif de l’infantile (1996), which was first published in French twenty-five years ago. In 2020, a new edition was released with two new chapters, an updated bibliography, and an index. It is this new, expanded edition that Routledge is now offering to the English-speaking public.

In this book, the analyst promotes the notion of the Infantile (with a capital “I”)—a notion derived directly from Freud but which she enriches using insights gleaned from her own practice and her own readings of post-Freudian psychoanalysis, most notably authors such as Bion, Klein, and Green. In a way, the book offers a new interpretation of Freud’s famous apothegm das Kind ist der Vater des Mannes, “The child is father to the man,”1 building on this interpretation to reflect on how to treat children, adolescents as well as adults.

An inventory of what was lost when psychoanalysis was forced into exile from its Central European birthplace remains uncompleted, but amongst that which was left behind certainly ranks its speculative tradition. The reverence shown Freud might have been enough to ensure that Totem and Taboo, Moses and Monotheism, and Beyond the Pleasure Principle continued to 143 be read, though the radical hypothesis of the death drive would quickly be reduced to the mere fact of instinctive aggression, and Moses read as a parable for its historical moment. Other authors fared still more poorly. Ferenczi’s foray into psychocatastrophism is largely passed over in embarrassed silence by even his most ardent contemporary partisans, and the metapsychological novels of Georg Groddeck are today all but forgotten.

The reasons for this abandonment belong to the postwar push to invent for psychoanalysis a certain scientific respectability. This entailed the disavowal, motivated by an adherence to the Darwinian Synthesis, of the idea that acquired traumatic experiences could be inherited biologically. But such Lamarckian assumptions were by no means essential to the speculative genre of psychoanalysis. Still more consequential would be the drawing of a hard distinction between the domains of analytic theory and practice. Theory would henceforth assume the role of a secondary account of the ostensibly hard data of the clinic. Operating within such a framework, which continues to underwrite contemporary controversies while itself remaining unexamined, there would be no place for ein historischer Roman, such as Freud dubbed Moses and Monotheism, nor for the scientific fantasies of phylogenetic processes, nor indeed for Groddeck’s comic presentation of psychoanalytic theory itself as a species of Witz. The inadmissibility of these works rest upon their deliberate and knowing transgression of the division drawn between fantasy as an object of clinical attention and the theory that gives an account of the symptomatic elements while itself remaining asymptomatic. To put it bluntly, postwar psychoanalysis aims to provide a transitional space in the clinic; transitional spaces are largely unwelcome in the domain of theory.

The psychoanalytic field continues to struggle with the dilemmas of conceptualizing gender and the experience of gender transition, even though gender appears to be very present in its multiple and transitional forms in the realm of the psyche as it manifests through the affective situation of the transference. In this paper, I want to move to an understanding of different situations of transitions that are grounded in gender but that suggest a wider world of experience with the claim that understanding the self is a complicated matter; and while this in itself is obvious to everyone, its complexity still comes as a surprise because of the unconscious. I turn to four memoirs: P. Carl’s Becoming a Man; Susan Faludi’s In the Darkroom; Masha Gessen’s “To Be or Not To Be”; and Jane Gallop’s Sexuality, Disability and Aging: Queer Temporalities of the Phallus. Each text depicts different notions of transition that suggest a wider world of experience: physicality (age, illness, disability), generation, sexuality, and relationality. In unpacking each narrative as unique figurations of transitioning, I show how each gives us a foothold into a new way of imagining gender. I argue that by reading memoirs the analyst enters a world that is theirs and not theirs. It is a way into an imaginative realm that allows us entrance into conflicts, questions, and representations of being in the world.

Past, present, memories, life history, repetition, transference, historicization, actualization, dehistoricization, posteriority, natality

Psychoanalysis focuses both on the patient’s inner life history and on what happens in the actual analytic situation. Psychoanalysts differ in the extent they pay attention to memories and the past or to the actuality of the analytic session as such and in the extent they link both. The main goal of this paper is to give an overview of ideas in the history of psychoanalytic thought on the relationship between past and present. The paper examines five possible positions: historicization (the past colors the present), actualization (back and forth between past and present), dehistoricization (the here and now), posteriority (the present colors the past), and natality (present without link with the past). New positions are added to old ones rather than replacing them. Together, all the positions testify to a lively dynamic in psychoanalysis that both repeats and transforms itself in everyday analytic thinking and practice.

We explored the dynamics of treatment termination in a patient with borderline personality organization who underwent eight years of transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP). A previous paper examined the beginnings of this treatment (Bernardi and Eidlin 2024). In this paper, the Primal Scene (PrS)—a par excellence primal phantasy, is considered in its function as a central scheme of the primordial psychic world, a kind of core template, which not only constraints the symbolizing urges of mental life “into certain channels” (Freud 1938, p. 187) but also canalizes, contains, and organizes them, thus furthering their elaboration. Myths, premature endings, returns, individualizing, mortality, older analysts, professional wills, mourning

There are many myths about how a psychoanalysis ends. In reality, there is no one way. In this paper, I describe what I learned from interviews with eighty-two analysands who volunteered to tell me about how they ended their analyses. Their experiences illustrate many different ways in which analyses end—some very satisfactory and others in disappointment. I also describe many different ways I have concluded psychoanalyses with my patients. I try to end each treatment to fit the needs of each patient and the nature of our work together. There are no formulas to how we end. I consider and explore the issues of being an older analyst: the risks and responsibilities of continuing to treat analytic—or any—patients. I discuss what we psychoanalysts gain from our work with patients—how it is sustaining and how we learn about ourselves as well as our patients. In doing psychoanalytic work with our patients, we stretch our own capacities and change. We, like our patients, though not to the same degree or intensity, mourn our endings.

Starting with the English translations of Freud’s 1937 nuanced concept of ending analysis, the author touches on the history of subsequent ego psychologists’ more exact notions of termination. Merton Gill’s radical shift in perspective away from that attempt, shows how more modern, post-1990 theoretical developments have evolved toward more subjective, intersubjective, and ranging judgments about what may be practical (Freud’s own final 1937 word). Resuming ego development as a goal, for example, and the role of analyst as new object (Loewald 1960 for example), is linked to a creative process of a patient’s increased subjective well-being—one feature of ending that cannot be precisely measured. There are two clinical examples of terminations: (1) The author’s experience of hearing Hanna Segal tell impressively about a case and its ending, circa 1970; (2) a longitudinal account of a four-part analytic involvement, from a patient’s teenage to middle years, that demonstrates different kinds of endings over a patient’s life. The last analysis, with a new analyst, after the original analyst’s death, was supervised by the author. Summed up, the termination phase is a deep study of the complexity of human existence for both analyst and analysand. This appreciation, including its limitations, helps many analysands fruitfully continue their life journey.

Reflections on the process of psychoanalytic termination led to reexamination of a long-term case of a person who experienced major dissociation in response to severe neglect in infancy and beyond. Her need to return one year after our ending led to a reconsideration of what ending is possible for our more traumatized patients. This essay also considers larger themes of aging, dying, and departure as they relate to increased access to aliveness in the present.

Disavowal is a small book that makes big claims. Zupančič develops her titular concept in order to explain a range of confounding sociopolitical phenomena—climate change denialism, proliferating conspiracy theories, the anti-vaccination movement, and a growing mistrust of scientific expertise in general. “Disavowal, which sustains some belief by means of ardently proclaiming the knowledge of the opposite, is becoming a predominant feature of our social and political life,” she contends (p. 2). Among her central claims is that disavowal—as distinct from repression, on one hand, or denial, on the other—should be understood as a “social rather than just individual structure” (p. 18). The book offers a philosophically sophisticated attempt to account for what can look like completely irrational developments. Zupančič insists that, far from irrational, “the contemporary social modality of disavowal is a perverse form of reason, of knowledge itself, and not a return of some archaic and obscure drive” (p. 3, original italics). At our bewildering historical moment, it may be worth considering the hypothesis that more than merely individual cluelessness or mass denial prompts millions of Americans to embrace Trumpian falsehoods, for example.

As a psychic defense mechanism, disavowal describes how people may at once acknowledge the facts and yet proceed as if in blithe ignorance of them. For example: Yes, we know that politicians always lie, but we nevertheless believe what Donald Trump says; or, we see the signs of global warming, but we still believe that “climate change” is a hoax. Over the summer, I was preparing a course on psychoanalytic couples therapy and was utilizing video clips from the TV series Couples Therapy, which features Orna Gurlanik. One of the couples in season four is polycule, so I searched the psychoanalytic literature for readings on polyamory. I was surprised to discover virtually no psychoanalytic writings dedicated to this topic, aside from an article by McCann1 that focuses on a type of nonmonogamy practiced by gay men, rather than polyamory specifically. A broader search yielded The Many Faces of Polyamory: Longing and Belonging in Concurrent Relationships, a book written by Magdelena Fosse in 2021. Though the book is theoretically eclectic rather than specifically psychoanalytic, it is a useful read for the psychoanalyst. Aside from the importance of being able to work with a broad range of patients, understanding polyamory can help analysts think more critically of monogamy, including its adaptive and defensive functions. It can also help analysts address mononormative biases. For example, in the wake of an affair, most psychoanalytic (and non-psychoanalytic) couple therapists strive to help the couple restore their monogamous state–-rarely do therapists help the couple reexamine and renegotiate the terms of their relationship. Dr. Fosse likens this mononormative bias to heteronormativity. She points out that increased attention and education about non-heterosexual orientations have helped redress this bias, and the same could be true for polyamory.

His scholarly and clinical research focuses on the intersection of psychoanalysis and neuroscience, especially Lacanian neuropsychoanalysis. He conducts empirical research on primary process in brain injury, psychological assessment, and on the teaching of neuropsychoanalysis in undergraduate education. He is the author of A Lacanian Neuropsychoanalysis: Consciousness Enjoying Uncertainty (2024, Palgrave) and Mark Solms: A Contemporary Introduction (forthcoming, Routledge).
Lacan, Freud, Solms, Neuropsychoanalysis, Vorstellung, Signifier

Lacan’s return to Freud gravitates around his aphorism that the unconscious is structured like a language. This is often cause for criticism from non-Lacanian analysts. However, this aphorism has multiple meanings beyond the unconscious consisting of word-forms. This paper sketches relational, affective, neuropsychological, and Freudian criticisms of this linguistic unconscious. I will then highlight that the key signifier is “like”: to be structured “like” a language is to be structured according to differential representatives. I conclude with a Lacanian neuropsychoanalytic functional model of differential representatives that need not be words.

Stephen D. Purcell   Faculty member at the San Francisco Center for Psychoanalysis, the Psychoanalytic Institute of Northern California, and the Oregon Psychoanalytic Institute.
Termination, coerced ending, retirement, illness in the analyst, long analysis, pandemic, remote analysis, finality, death, trauma, clinical theory

The author describes and reflects upon his clinical experiences with both mutually desired terminations and coerced endings. He addresses issues of technique, being real in termination and post-termination contact in addition to offering his perspectives on the role of theory in determining the phenomena of termination, retraumatizing aspects of termination, termination and death, and the question of whether analytic relationships could or should be ended.
